sounds.intro: Czech is written in the Latin alphabet with accents. It is spelled almost exactly as it sounds. Nouns have three genders and seven cases. The stress is always on the first syllable of a word.
rows: roll an "r" and say "zh" at the same time, a sound only Czech has
á / é / í / ó / ú / ů / ý
a soft "d", "t" or "n" with the tongue pressed to the palate
notes: Czech has long and short vowels. A long vowel has an accent (á, é, í, ó, ú, ý) or a ring (ů). Length changes the word.
Some words have no vowel. "r" and "l" can be a vowel: krk (throat), vlk (wolf).

grammar.title: Pronouns
text: Czech often drops the pronoun, because the verb ending shows who is speaking. "On" is he, "ona" is she, "ono" is it. "Ty" is informal and "vy" is formal.

grammar.title: Singular and plural
text: The ending changes with gender. Feminine -a becomes -y: kniha, knihy. Masculine often adds -y or -i: dům, domy. Neuter -o becomes -a: město, města. After 5 and higher, the noun takes a different form.

grammar.title: To be: být
text: "Být" (to be) is irregular. Learn all the forms. The pronoun is usually dropped.

grammar.title: Mít: have
text: "Mít" (to have): mám, máš, má, máme, máte, mají. "Je" or "jsou" also means "there is".

grammar.title: Present tense
text: The ending shows the person. Pracovat (to work): pracuji, pracuješ, pracuje, pracujeme, pracujete, pracují.

grammar.title: Basic sentences
text: The usual order is who, verb, what, but Czech is flexible. There are no articles: "kniha" means "a book" or "the book".

grammar.title: Negation
text: Put "ne-" in front of the verb: mám (I have), nemám (I do not have). Czech uses double negatives: nikdy nic nevím.
ex: I do not have a car
he does not work on Sundays

grammar.title: Asking questions
text: The word order does not change. Just raise your voice at the end. You can also start with "Je to ...?"

grammar.title: Question words
text: Question words stand at the start of the sentence.

grammar.title: Possessives and liking
text: The word agrees with the noun: můj / moje / mé (my), tvůj / tvoje (your), jeho (his), její (her), náš / naše (our), váš / vaše (your, formal), jejich (their). To like something, say "mám rád" (I have ... glad) or "líbí se mi".

grammar.title: Formal vs informal
text: ty (informal): friends, family, children. vy (formal): strangers, older people, work. The verb changes: -š (informal), -te (formal). Czechs use "vy" more than English speakers expect.
rows: jak se máš? / jak se máte?
yak seh mahsh / yak seh MAH-teh

grammar.title: Past and future (simple)
text: Past: the stem + -l + a form of "to be": byl jsem (I was). Future: "budu" + the basic verb: budu pracovat (I will work).

grammar.title: Commands
text: Informal: the stem (pojď). Formal and plural: add -te (pojďte). To forbid, put "ne-" in front: nechoď.

grammar.title: Can, must, want
text: Moci (can): mohu / můžu. Muset (must): musím. Chtít (want): chci. The second verb stays in its basic form.
ex: I do not want to eat

grammar.title: In, on, at
text: Czech uses small words, and the noun changes its ending after them: v (in), na (on), u (at, by), do (to, into), z (from), s (with), pod (under).
ex: the book is on the table
the cat is under the table
the shop is next to the bank
the park is near the station
the key is in the bag

grammar.title: Comparing things
text: Add -ější / -ší for "more": velký, větší (irregular). For "the most" put "nej-" in front: největší. "Than" is "než".
